content.thinking:
I need to keep the momentum of the prototype while the npm install runs in the background. The user wants a hyper‑realistic tactical shooter, but for now I’m delivering a functional web‑based prototype using three.js and Vite. I’ve already created the project scaffold (package.json) and kicked off the dependency install, so the next logical step is to add the HTML entry point that will host the canvas and the HUD elements.

First, I should consider what the HTML needs to contain:
- A minimal but complete document structure (<!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, <body>).
- Meta tags for charset and viewport to ensure proper scaling on all devices.
- A <title> that reflects the game name (“KILLHOUSE — Tactical CQB”) to give it a polished feel.
- A <style> block that defines the base layout, resets, and the full‑screen canvas styling. Since I’m not using external CSS files yet, embedding the styles directly keeps the prototype self‑contained.
- The HUD: crosshair, hitmarker, health bar, ammo display, objective counter, compass, killfeed, and vignette. All of these should be positioned with CSS, hidden or shown via classes, and use simple HTML elements (divs and spans) to avoid extra dependencies.
- Screens for menu, game over, and victory states, each with appropriate headings, instructions, and a prompt to click. These will be toggled via JavaScript later.
- Finally, I need to load the main JavaScript module (src/main.js) using a <script type="module"> tag, which Vite will serve.

I also need to make sure the IDs and class names match what the upcoming JavaScript will expect (e.g., #hud, #crosshair, #hitmarker, #healthfill, #magcount, #reservecount, #killfeed, etc.). Consistency is crucial to avoid runtime errors.

Given that the dependencies are still installing, I should avoid any heavy assets or external fonts; using system fonts like “Segoe UI” and “Roboto” will be sufficient for now. The CSS should include a reset (margin, padding, box-sizing) and set html/body to full width/height with overflow hidden to prevent scrollbars.

I’ll also add a simple background color (#000) for the body, and style the canvas to be block‑level so it fills the container. The HUD will start invisible (opacity: 0) and become visible once the game starts; the transition will be handled via CSS.

For the crosshair and hitmarker, I’ll use small <span> elements positioned absolutely within a parent div, with simple rectangular shapes and slight opacity changes. The crosshair should disappear when aiming down sights (ADS), so I’ll add an .ads class that sets opacity to 0.

The health bar will consist of a container (#healthbar) and a fill element (#healthfill) whose width will be updated by JS. The ammo panel will show the magazine count, reserve count, weapon name, and a reload hint that is hidden by default.

The compass will be a strip of text that scrolls horizontally; I’ll set up a container (#compass) and an inner div (#compass-strip) for the dynamic content.

The killfeed will be a simple container where each kill entry is appended as a div, with a fade‑out animation defined via @keyframes.

Screens (menu, gameover, victory) will be full‑screen overlays with centered text, using the .screen class. The menu will be visible initially, while the others start hidden (class .hidden). Each screen includes a prompt that blinks to indicate interactivity.

All of this can be expressed in a single HTML file, which Vite will serve at the root. I’ll write the file to D:\fps\index.html with the exact content prepared, ensuring proper indentation and line breaks for readability.

Now I’ll issue the Write tool call with the path and the full HTML content I just assembled.
